papers.title: Probabilistic Upscaling of the Interfacial Transition Zone Behaviour in Concrete
papers.abstract: The stiffness and cracking behaviour of concrete are influenced by the interfacial transition zone (ITZ), the thin shell of paste that surrounds each aggregate. Yet the ITZ's mechanical properties are poorly characterized and are usually assigned to mesoscale models through ad hoc reduction factors. Because the ITZ is only tens of micrometres thick, its stiffness must be inferred indirectly from micromechanical tests, and the resulting estimates vary widely between studies and are rarely reported with a quantified uncertainty. We present a workflow that calibrates a homogenized ITZ model against the surface displacements of several micro-cantilever bending specimens and returns its stiffness descriptors as posterior distributions rather than single values. The calibration is posed as a Bayesian inverse problem with a model-discrepancy term, sampled with a surrogate-assisted Bouncy Particle sampler, the first application of this sampler to a real-world engineering problem. We compare a pooled model, which fits one descriptor vector to all specimens, with a hierarchical model that treats the specimens as draws from a common population and is sampled with a local extension of the sampler. The hierarchical model separates the estimation uncertainty from the aggregate-to-aggregate material variability, where only the former shrinks as more data are added. Propagated through a representative volume element of several aggregates, its predictive yields broader distributions of the mesoscale stress and strain and a wider spread variety of maximum von Mises stress locations. The calibration places the ITZ thickness above the 30 {\mu}m to 80 {\mu}m commonly assumed in the literature.

papers.title: Universal Multichannel Coherence-Mediated Thermal Transport in Carbon Allotropes: Experimental Evidence and Scaling Laws
papers.abstract: Understanding thermal transport in structurally disordered carbon materials remains a fundamental challenge because conventional models based on a single coherence contribution cannot accurately describe heat conduction over a broad temperature range. In this work, the thermal conductivity of graphene oxide (GO), thermally reduced graphene oxide (trGO), GO-hydrated fullerene composites (GO-HyFn), expanded graphite (EG), and EG-multiwalled carbon nanotube (MWCNT) composites was measured between 4.5 and 300 K. Despite substantial differences in density, porosity, graphitic ordering, and microstructure, all materials exhibit glass-like temperature dependence of thermal conductivity. The experimental results demonstrate that the conventional two-channel model, comprising a Peierls contribution and a single thermally activated coherence term, systematically fails to reproduce the observed temperature dependence. To resolve this discrepancy, we propose a generalized multichannel phenomenological model in which the coherence contribution consists of up to three Arrhenius-type channels with distinct activation energies. Depending on the structural state, two or three coherence channels are required to accurately describe the thermal conductivity. A key finding is the reproducible hierarchy of activation energies across diverse carbon allotropes, following approximately (E2 ~ 4E1 and E3 ~ (12-25)E1). While the channel amplitudes increase with material density, the activation energies remain nearly invariant, indicating universal vibrational energy scales. The proposed framework also consistently describes published data for other disordered carbon materials. These results provide experimental evidence for multichannel coherence-mediated heat transport and establish a unified phenomenological bridge between structural hierarchy with thermal transport in disordered carbon solids.

papers.title: Geometric regulation of stress-limited growth on surfaces
papers.abstract: We analyze a model for microbial communities growing on surfaces in which individual growth is inhibited by collective growth-induced pressure. Asymptotic and numerical solutions on the sphere and homogenization of periodic surfaces show surface geometry can be tuned to either slow or accelerate growth. We use these insights to identify classes of surfaces for which the growth rate can be made arbitrarily small or arbitrarily close to the stress-free growth rate. These results show stress-sensing is coupled to surface curvature and topography at scales much larger than the individual, and provide design principles for controlling the growth of stress-sensitive microbial communities.

papers.title: Neural network scaling and generalization for 3D strain fields in heterogeneous materials
papers.abstract: Computational homogenization and coupled multiscale simulations of heterogeneous materials require repeated solution of mechanical fields on Representative Volume Elements, which becomes prohibitively expensive for high-resolution three-dimensional microstructures. Machine-learning surrogates can accelerate these computations, yet most existing approaches predict fields for fixed macroscopic loadings and provide limited guidance on how to scale network architectures for high-resolution 3D tensor-field prediction. This work presents a U-Net surrogate trained to predict the full 36-component strain localization tensor field in voxelized concrete mesostructures at resolutions up to $256^3$. Training localization tensors are generated with an FFT-based linear elastic solver, and an extensive hyperparameter optimization is performed to derive scaling rules and an accuracy-speed trade-off analysis. The results show that only network width and depth need to be scaled with problem complexity, while several conventional U-Net design choices, such as doubling channels after downsampling, are suboptimal for this problem. The final neural network achieves a Mean Absolute Error of 1.118% on both the validation and the held-out test sets, and an inference speedup of approximately 8.7x over the FFT-based solver on an Nvidia H100 GPU. Generalization experiments reveal transfer across aggregate volume fractions and highlight the importance of training on diverse morphologies. To safeguard reliability, a Maximum Mean Discrepancy metric computed on internal feature maps is proposed for detecting out-of-distribution microstructures without costly reference computations.

papers.title: End-state-assisted tunneling at a topological insulator STM tip
papers.abstract: Recent spin-sensitive scanning tunneling experiments with topological-insulator tips motivate a microscopic understanding of how tip geometry controls current delivery. We show that topological end states mediate resonant tunneling through the gap opened by interedge hybridization in a quantum spin Hall tip. An asymmetric termination gives oppositely spin-polarized helical paths unequal effective lengths and resonance widths. Within an independent-path description, their transmitted-current imbalance vanishes at a matched resonance and becomes finite away from it. Coupling these directional channels to a $d$-wave altermagnet yields a spin-dependent interference contrast. Hybridized end states along a stepped termination provide multiple tunneling resonances. Our results establish end-state-mediated tunneling as a transport mechanism for STM with strongly confined topological tips.

papers.title: Where are the shortest-path nodes in spatial networks?
papers.abstract: To predict the spatial distribution of shortest-path nodes, we propose a Gaussian estimate of the shortest-path node probability $\pi_{uv}(w)$, the probability that a node $w$ lies on a shortest path between a source $u$ and a destination $v$. According to the Gaussian estimate, three variables affect the shortest-path node probability $\pi_{uv}(w)$ and combine into one variable, the standardized detour $X_{uvw}$. In our simulations of hard and soft random geometric graphs in Euclidean, hyperbolic and spherical space, the standardized detour $X_{uvw}$ alone approximately determines how fast the shortest-path node probability $\pi_{uv}(w)$ decreases as the node $w$ moves away from the geodesic between the source $u$ and the destination $v$. We find and explain that, when the hopcount variance $\sigma^2(H_{uv})$ is very small, the shortest-path nodes have a discrete spatial distribution, a quantized distribution of shortest-path nodes. We further extend the study to spatially inhomogeneous networks, for which we propose a method to find the shortest-path nodes.

papers.title: Limits of Cell Sensing in Observer-Absorber Assemblies
papers.abstract: Absorption improves concentration sensing for an isolated cell by suppressing rebinding correlations. We study how that local advantage competes with collective depletion in assemblies of cells coupled through the shared diffusion field. We introduce an observer--absorber model for permeant ligands sensed and consumed intracellularly with finite volumetric uptake rate $\kappa$ that continuously interpolates between Berg--Purcell monitoring and perfect absorption. For a single spherical cell, monitoring correlations, uptake statistics and optimal joint estimator are obtained analytically, and we characterize the transition between using observer and absorber information for sensing. In this case, all sensing strategies improve monotonically with $\kappa$. For arbitrary cell assemblies, we show that the long-time sensing problem can be reduced to solving for just two steady-state quantities for each cell: the mean internal concentration $\Cbar$ and its local sensitivity $\Tbar=-\partial_{\kappa}\log\Cbar$. In multicellular systems, uptake shortens rebinding memory, but it also depletes the signal available to neighbors. We reveal geometry-dependent optima for absorption rates, with Pareto fronts arising from competing objectives, as well as pure observing, pure absorbing, and partially absorbing regimes.

papers.title: Estimating multidimensional poverty under incomplete data in North Macedonia
papers.abstract: Multidimensional Poverty Indices (MPIs) are available for more than 100 countries, but rarely below the national or regional level. Local estimates require knowing how deprivations overlap within households, yet the sources that cover every locality, such as censuses and geospatial data, cannot be linked at the household level. We show how to measure local multidimensional poverty under such incomplete data, using North Macedonia as a case study. Combining settlement-level access to services with municipal census data, we pair an independence-based point estimate with sharp bounds over all joint distributions consistent with the data. We find that, nationally, 5.01 percent of households are multidimensionally poor, with bounds of 2.01 to 17.44 percent. Also, poverty is concentrated in small rural municipalities, which are poorer than nearly all municipalities of the capital city under any dependence structure. Validating our index against official statistics, the Global MPI, and a fieldwork deprivation index indicates that the socio-economic part of the index is consistent with external measures of deprivation, while the geographic part captures a distinct dimension of remoteness. Our approach thus presents a promising way to measure multidimensional poverty at the local level in countries where linked household data are unavailable.

papers.title: Energetic costs of reaching the physical limits of sensing
papers.abstract: Cells sense chemical gradients by absorbing ligand molecules, a nonequilibrium process that necessarily produces entropy. But how many molecules must a cell absorb, and therefore energy dissipate, to approach the physical limits of sensing? We derive closed-form expressions relating gradient sensing uncertainty to the number of absorbed molecules, which we link to entropy production. Unlike concentration sensing, which depends only on the total count, gradient sensing must resolve the angular asymmetry of the absorbed flux, adding a bounded dipole-contrast factor set by how strongly the cell absorbs. In the strong-signal regime, cells approach peak chemotactic alignment while absorbing a small fraction of the diffusion-limited uptake, with the required number of uptake events set by the relative concentration change across the cell. Re-analysis of Dictyostelium chemotaxis places the cell at 0.25% of that limit with a minor metabolic load, suggesting that sensing is limited by counting noise rather than by energetic cost.

papers.title: Exponential Control of Adiabatic Time Reflection by Complex-Time Singularities
papers.abstract: Nearly identical temporal switching profiles can produce very different reflections even when both have small local adiabatic measures. In a lossless dielectric, we obtain this difference by adding a weak feature that changes the complex-time singularities while preserving monotonicity, endpoints, and central slope. A perturbation bounded by $0.6\%$ of the total inverse-permittivity change raises the reflected mode amplitude from $8.02\times10^{-10}$ to $1.28\times10^{-3}$. The complex action and pole residue predict this amplitude to within $0.32\%$. Within this waveform family, deviation and monotonicity constraints select three design regimes. At fixed deviation bound, reoptimization keeps the central feature's time scale comparable to the inverse incident angular frequency. The optimal amplitude is then proportional to $1/T$ as the switching time $T$ tends to infinity. Stretching a fixed profile gives exponential suppression. Full-wave Maxwell simulations resolve the backward packet, and filtering calculations quantify its sensitivity to modulation bandwidth.

papers.title: Mesoscopic derivation of predator-prey dynamics via diffusive fast-reaction asymptotics: cross-diffusion and fear effects
papers.abstract: We propose a kinetic derivation of a spatial predator-prey model with cross-diffusion interactions and a Beddington-DeAngelis functional response. At the mesoscopic level, we divide the two populations into distinct behavioral states: prey can be active or hidden in a refuge, while predators can be either searching or handling. The microscopic state of each subpopulation is described in terms of group size and a continuous directional velocity variable, with state transitions governed by suitable Boltzmann-type interaction operators. By combining a diffusive scaling with a slow-fast formulation of the kinetic reaction operators, we formally derive a macroscopic reaction-cross-diffusion system for the total population densities of prey and predators. The limiting model consistently recovers the Beddington-DeAngelis functional response along with its associated nonlinear diffusion terms. Crucially, the kinetic upscaling yields a predator-dependent prey growth term taking a logistic form with an effective carrying capacity. This carrying capacity depends non-monotonically on predator density because prey redistribute between active and refuge states. Since density-dependent competition acts separately within these behavioral states, intermediate predator levels reduce aggregate crowding and thereby increase the effective carrying capacity of the total prey population. Overall, our derivation provides a mechanistic link connecting predator-induced behavioral shifts, refuge use, and macroscopic cross-diffusion.

papers.title: Cohesive granular piles with controlled volume fraction
papers.abstract: Experimental procedures involving wet granular media expose the sample to variation of its organization across different measurements, leading to non reproducible results. Rigorous control over the preparation process and a thorough understanding of the microstructure of the granular heap are key parameters to manage results dispersion from one experiment to an other. In this study, we present a protocol to prepare large samples of wet grains in a cylindrical container. Quantitative results are presented showing the effectiveness of the protocol regarding : the accessibility of different granular materials with different volume fraction $\phi_0$ and the reproducibility of this said density obtained experimentally in the same experimental conditions. In addition, X-ray scans were performed using a micro-CT scanner to dive into the microstructure of the carefully prepared piles. Results show a small variation between the bulk density $\phi_0$ and the local one $\phi$, underlining the homogeneity in the samples. On top of that, several scans made in the same medium at different heights confirm the homogeneity across a given sample.

papers.title: Mechanical pairing and self-assembled chains of non-convex granular rotors
papers.abstract: We experimentally and numerically demonstrate the self-assembly of granular rotors into chain-like structures. The rotors are non-convex rigid bodies with rotational activity. We first investigate the interaction between two rotors and we establish an attractive interaction controlled by the ratio of the rotational activity to the noise and also dependent of the rotors geometry. We then show that the cohesive state between spinner pairs leads to robust chains that can be either initially set or spontaneously obtained by self-assembly.

papers.title: Physics-informed Bayesian optimization of high-order harmonic generation in gases
papers.abstract: Optimization of high-order harmonic generation in gases is essential for attosecond science. Improving conversion efficiency from the infrared driving laser to the extreme-ultraviolet high-order harmonic radiation requires balancing microscopic single-atom dipole responses with macroscopic phase matching. The resulting conversion-efficiency landscape exhibits complex structures, such as the hyperbolic ridge in the pressure-length space, which can be difficult to accurately reconstruct using conventional Bayesian optimization. Here, we introduce a physics-informed Bayesian optimization framework that incorporates known physical scaling relations through nonlinear transformations of the search space. We first demonstrate the approach in the two-dimensional pressure-length space, where a direct grid scan enables detailed validation of the reconstructed landscape, before extending it to four dimensions, where exhaustive scanning becomes computationally impractical. In four dimensions, incorporating the pulse-duration scaling and a square-root transformation of conversion efficiency further improves the accuracy of the reconstructed landscape, as validated against an independent reference dataset. We also employ a threshold-based acquisition strategy to identify extended high-efficiency operating regions rather than isolated optimal points. Together, these results demonstrate that incorporating physical knowledge into Bayesian optimization improves the exploration and reconstruction of multidimensional high-order harmonic generation landscapes, extending its capabilities beyond locating individual optima.

papers.title: SGAA: Independent active alignment of optical subgroups with uncompensated aberrations
papers.abstract: Uncompensated subgroup aberrations complicate subgroup-level active alignment (AA), as local image-quality extrema do not directly indicate the target alignment state. We propose SGAA, an image-learning-based method for independent active alignment of optical subgroups. Multi-field point spread functions (PSFs) from a dedicated test configuration characterize misalignment, while golden-sample reference calibration and unified regression predict adjustments toward a common optical target across toleranced specimens. In simulations with tolerances, one step reduced the mean differential wavefront RMS from $0.0592\lambda$ to $0.0086\lambda$, an 85.4% reduction. In alignment experiments on 100 production subgroups, SGAA increased the mean full-lens weighted modulation transfer function (WMTF) at 30, 50, and 80 lp/mm by 0.073, 0.065, and 0.040, respectively, relative to industrial MTF-based scanning. The 8 MP acceptance yield increased by 29.2 percentage points, and mean alignment time decreased from 43 s to 3.1 s. SGAA thus translates independent subgroup reference-state restoration into gains in full-lens imaging, acceptance yield, and alignment speed.

papers.title: Spin-glass order in a field requires magnetic-field chaos in XY gauge glasses for $d\leq 4$
papers.abstract: The XY gauge-glass model is believed to exhibit a spin-glass phase in dimensions $d\geq 3$. In this paper, we prove that, in dimensions $d\leq 4$ and at any finite temperature, a magnetic field applied in a fixed direction, with amplitudes that fluctuate from site to site according to the Rayleigh distribution, must either induce magnetic-field chaos in the spin-glass phase or destroy spin-glass order altogether, whenever a spin-glass phase exists at zero field. In particular, if a spin-glass phase persists under such a field, as predicted by the replica-symmetry-breaking (RSB) picture, it must exhibit magnetic-field chaos. This conclusion follows from our proof that, for any fixed nonzero field strength, the disorder average of the squared overlap between equilibrium spin configurations at zero field and those at nonzero field vanishes in the thermodynamic limit. By gauge transformations, the overlap statistics are identical to the magnetization statistics of an XY gauge glass with correlated bond disorder in a Gaussian random field. Our proof combines this exact identity with quantitative estimates on the suppression of ferromagnetic order by random fields in continuous-spin systems, due to Dario, Harel, and Peled [Commun. Math. Phys. 405, 212 (2024)] and building on the work of Imry and Ma [Phys. Rev. Lett. 35, 1399 (1975)] and of Aizenman and Wehr [Phys. Rev. Lett. 62, 2503 (1989); Commun. Math. Phys. 130, 489 (1990)]. We extend these estimates to bond-dependent interactions. Although our result provides a rare rigorous constraint on the nature of spin-glass phases in finite-dimensional systems, it does not determine whether spin-glass order survives in a field, and therefore does not distinguish between the droplet and RSB pictures. The case of a strictly uniform field remains open.

papers.title: Memory of Initial States in Long-Time Dynamics Revealed by Non-Gaussianity
papers.abstract: In quantum dynamics of few-body observables in quadratic systems, information about the initial state is retained in long-time averages, as captured by the generalized Gibbs ensemble. Here, we show that this memory extends beyond the averages to temporal fluctuations around them. By generating a manifold of non-Gaussian initial states and quantifying their non-Gaussianity via the corresponding entropy, we find that the magnitude of temporal fluctuations is a smooth function of the initial-state non-Gaussianity. This relation explains the qualitatively different scaling of fluctuations observed after quantum quenches: exponentially small fluctuations for non-Gaussian initial states and polynomially small fluctuations for Gaussian initial states. Therefore, our results identify non-Gaussianity as a key to uncovering initial-state memory beyond long-time averages.

papers.title: Purely elastic centre-mode instability in channel and pipe flows of a simplified Phan-Thien-Tanner fluid
papers.abstract: Recent work identified spatially localised midplane stress structures as the building blocks of chaotic behaviour in pressure-driven parallel shear flows of viscoelastic fluids. Such coherent structures are thought to originate from a linear centre-mode instability of the laminar state. In the absence of inertia, however, the Oldroyd-B and FENE-P constitutive models predict that this instability is confined to ultra-dilute polymer solutions and very large Weissenberg numbers in channel flow, while no purely elastic instability has been reported in pipe flow. Here, we study numerically the linear stability of channel and pipe flows of a simplified Phan-Thien-Tanner (sPTT) fluid and find a purely elastic centre-mode instability in both geometries across a wide range of polymer concentrations and at much lower Weissenberg numbers. Since the sPTT and FENE-P models have identical steady rheology and laminar profiles, their contrasting predictions indicate that the existence of the centre-mode instability is governed by the transient rheological response of the fluid. Our results suggest that the purely elastic centre-mode instability should be observable under realistic flow conditions. They also offer a means of discriminating between constitutive models.

papers.title: Nucleon sigma terms in lattice QCD at physical pion mass and in the continuum
papers.abstract: We determine the light, strange and charm $\sigma$-terms of the nucleon in lattice QCD using four $N_f=2+1+1$ twisted-mass gauge ensembles simulated at physical pion masses and with approximately the same spatial volumes. The four lattice spacings ranging from $0.080$ fm to $0.049$ fm, with an action that has O(a) improvement, enable extrapolating the results to the continuum limit. Both valence and sea quark contributions are analysed accounting for excited-state contamination from low-lying multihadron states. We perform global fits to all ensembles, that yield $\sigma_{\pi N}=53.0(7.4)(1.6)$ MeV, $\sigma_s=58.2(17.0)(2.1)$ MeV and $\sigma_c=112(28)(25)$ MeV, with statistical and systematic uncertainties, respectively.

papers.title: Particle-hole asymmetry and a fluctuating pair-density-wave state in a lightly doped Mott insulator on the square lattice
papers.abstract: Whether a lightly doped Mott insulator on the square lattice supports robust $d$-wave superconductivity remains a central question in strongly correlated physics and in the microscopic theory of cuprate superconductivity. Experiments and numerical studies reveal a pronounced particle-hole asymmetry, pointing to a delicate competition among $d$-wave superconductivity, pair-density wave (PDW), stripe, charge-density wave (CDW), and antiferromagnetic correlations. Here we combine large-scale DMRG and finite-size PEPS to study the square-lattice $t$-$J$ model at low doping, $\delta \leq 0.1$, while tuning the next-nearest-neighbor hopping $t'$ from the electron-like ($t'>0$) to the hole-like ($t'<0$) regime. The electron-like side supports robust, nearly uniform $d$-wave pairing, whereas decreasing $t'$ induces a period-two plaquette modulation and ultimately produces, on the hole-like side, a charge-dominated state with a strongly suppressed static pairing amplitude. DMRG calculations on open strips and squares, together with PEPS calculations on open squares up to $16\times16$ sites, support this evolution. On squares with $C_4$-symmetric Hamiltonians, both methods find that the pair correlations of the hole-like state select the plaquette momenta $(\pi,0)$ and $(0,\pi)$ and decay within a few lattice spacings, while the dominant charge-density modulation forms a bidirectional checkerboard whose period extrapolates to about $4a_0$, close to that observed in lightly doped Bi-2201. These observations establish a fluctuating plaquette PDW in the lightly doped hole-like regime, in which local pairs carry finite momentum but lack phase coherence. Our results firmly establish particle-hole asymmetry as a central organizing principle for competing pairing tendencies in the lightly doped $t$-$J$ model.

papers.title: A Kato-Type Criterion for Vanishing Viscosity and Magnetic Diffusivity Limits for Compressible Magnetohydrodynamics
papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate the vanishing viscosity and magnetic diffusivity limits for the compressible magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) equations on a smooth bounded domain in $\mathbb{R}^3$. Under the assumptions of interior regularity and uniform local boundedness near the boundary, we establish a Kato-type criterion under which finite energy weak solutions to the dissipative MHD system converge to weak solutions to the ideal MHD system as the viscosity and magnetic resistivity coefficients decrease to zero. In particular, under such criterion, the anomalous energy dissipation in the vanishing viscosity and diffusivity limits for MHD is precluded.

papers.title: Modelling velocity gradient invariants in turbulence with Lundgren spiral vortex ensemble
papers.abstract: We investigate the joint probability density function $P(Q,R)$ of invariants $Q$ and $R$ of the velocity gradient tensor in the synthetic turbulent field formed from the Lundgren spiral vortex ensemble, which is referred to as the woven Lundgren turbulence (WLT). The WLT inherently captures non-Gaussian vorticity correlations and multiscale interactions, which are essential for reproducing $P(Q,R)$ observed in homogeneous isotropic turbulence. By analyzing the contributions of stretching, winding and dissipation processes in WLT, we demonstrate that the $Q$-$R$ diagram can be divided into three distinct physical regions: a head region dominated by stretching, a body region dominated by spiral vortex arms, and a tail region dominated by dissipation. We systematically vary three key parameters in WLT, the background strain rate, the cutoff age of spiral vortices and the viscous decay factor, and monitor the evolution of $P(Q,R)$ in different topological regions. It is revealed that increasing the stretching rate broadens the head region, larger cutoff ages enhance the inclination of the body region, and reducing viscous factors extends the tail region, thereby mimicking the effects of strain self-amplification and vortex stretching across scales. Based on WLT statistics, we establish and validate an explicit model of $P(Q,R)$ consisting of the stretching, spiral and dissipation contributions. Thus, the WLT provides a physically interpretable framework for understanding the relation between local geometry and global statistics of turbulence.

papers.title: And yet it moves - or does it? Spurious drifts at equilibrium
papers.abstract: When diffusion depends on the state of a system, the drift measured from its trajectories contains a spurious part unrelated to forces. At equilibrium, particles can then appear to sediment, repel each other, even rotate - the same way whether the movie is played forward or backward. Drifts are conditional averages, not currents: they carry meaning only together with a consistently inferred diffusion tensor. Paired with the wrong one, they make passive particles look active. I show how to infer spurious drifts from trajectory moments alone, enabling thermodynamically consistent inference.

papers.title: Discrete-Time Stochastic Control Beyond i.i.d. Noise
papers.abstract: We study discrete-time stochastic control problems where the noise driving the state dynamics is a stationary infinite-order chain rather than an i.i.d. sequence. We formulate the problem as a controlled Markov process by enlarging the state space to include the posterior distribution of the noise given the state-action history. Assuming that the sensitivity of the noise transition kernel to past noise values decays exponentially, we show that the expected total variation distance between the full-history and finite-memory noise filters decays at rate $\sqrt{N}\rho^{\sqrt{N}}$. We use this result to construct finite-memory control models and establish explicit near-optimality bounds for their policies. Finally, under suitable ergodicity conditions, we show that Q-learning converges to the optimal solution of the approximate model, so the same performance bounds apply to the learned policies.

papers.title: Two atoms with strong light-induced dipolar interactions
papers.abstract: We study how two atoms scatter light when they are closer than an optical wavelength and observe multiple new phenomena due to the strong interactions between laser-induced electric dipole moments. We identify a narrow range of densities where a fraction of the scattered light is coherent and shows a collective enhancement factor of two compared to independent atoms. The dynamics of the two-atom wavefunction can be observed through momentum distributions which reveal resonant ejection and depletion. Due to the tight confinement, the total fluorescence intensity strongly depends on the scattering length, since it originates from a narrow resonant (Franck-Condon) region. Furthermore, we measure how the probe laser intensity modifies the scattering length, which establishes a new way to shift Feshbach resonances. Our work provides microscopic insight into what occurs during photoassociation and parity projection in optical tweezers.

papers.title: Landau Theory of Black-Brane Phase Transitions from Kasner Singularities
papers.abstract: We develop a Landau theory of a continuous black-brane phase transition using the geometry of the black-hole interior. The normal phase has a Reissner--Nordström Cauchy horizon, whereas the scalarized phase ends at a Kasner singularity. A conserved radial charge determines the grand potential from either endpoint and permits a direct phase comparison. At the critical point, we show analytically that the quadratic correction to the conserved radial charge vanishes. Using the inverse Kasner scalar velocity as an interior order parameter, we then construct a Landau potential whose coefficients are determined entirely from the terminal singularity. The Iyer--Wald first law relates this potential to the conventional boundary Landau theory and fixes its quartic coefficient. For two models with different scalar self-interactions, the resulting theory predicts the critical scaling of the Kasner order parameter and the grand-potential difference between the phases, in agreement with fully backreacted numerical solutions.

papers.title: Local electronic structure of the Co2+ ions in the disordered perovskite phase of Ba3CoNb2O9: a temperature-dependent X-ray absorption and magnetic circular dichroism study
papers.abstract: We performed temperature-dependent X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) and X-ray magnetic circular dichroism (XMCD) measurements on the disordered phase of Ba$_3$CoNb$_2$O$_9$ to determine the local electronic structure of the Co$^{2+}$ ions. We employed the line-fitting inverse partial fluorescence yield (iPFY) method to obtain reliable spectra from this insulating material. From the comparison between the experimental spectra and full multiplet cluster calculations we were able to constrain the local crystal-field environment and assess the spin-orbit-entangled nature of the Co$^{2+}$ ground state. In this chemically disordered system, the Co$^{2+}$ ions retain on average an effectively cubic crystal-field environment that supports a $J_\mathrm{eff} = 1/2$ ground state. These results further establish that Ba$_3$CoNb$_2$O$_9$ is a promising platform for investigating the effect of disorder on $J_\mathrm{eff} = 1/2$ magnetism.

papers.title: Evidence of anomalous Hall crystals in moiré rhombohedral graphene
papers.abstract: An anomalous Hall crystal (AHC) is a quantum state of matter, in which spontaneous electron crystallization leads to a quantized Hall effect without a magnetic field. The state can emerge in materials with strong Coulomb interaction and large Berry curvatures, such as few-layer rhombohedral graphene. Although the idea of AHCs has been invoked to explain some of the observed Chern insulators in moiré rhombohedral graphene (mRG), direct experimental evidence of AHCs has been missing so far. Here, we report experimental evidence of AHCs in hole-doped mRG through combined electrical transport and noise measurements. We identify a series of distinct Chern insulators spanning a broad and continuous range of doping densities incommensurate with the underlying moiré lattice; the states exhibit current-induced broadband noise and memory effects as well as pronounced gate hysteresis. Systematic magnetic field, temperature and gate dependence studies further support the emergence of a spontaneously charge-ordered state that acts as a parental state for the observed Chern insulators. The absence of Chern insulators at nearby integer fillings also distinguishes the observed state from the reported reentrant or extended quantum (anomalous) Hall states. Altogether, our results establish experimental evidence of AHCs in mRG and open the door for further exploration of the collective dynamics in this new state of matter.

papers.title: CURRENT: A Recurrent Neural Network for Concurrent Spatial and Temporal Super-Resolution of 4D Flow MRI
papers.abstract: Objective: To improve the spatial and temporal resolution of aortic 4D flow MRI through a unified deep learning framework for post-acquisition super-resolution (SR) of reconstructed velocity vector fields. Methods: We propose CURRENT, a recurrent neural network that performs spatial and temporal SR with a single network architecture. Supervised training was conducted using paired low- and high-resolution datasets generated by embedding computational fluid dynamics simulations of aortic flow into in vivo thoracic MRI backgrounds, followed by controlled spatial and temporal downsampling. CURRENT was evaluated for two-fold spatial and temporal SR against 4DFlowNet and for two-fold spatiotemporal SR against sequential spatial and temporal SR pipelines based on 4DFlowNet. Image-based and k-space-based quantitative metrics were considered and conventional interpolation were used as baselines. In addition, the impact of CURRENT's spatiotemporal SR on physics-informed relative pressure estimation was assessed. Finally, the ability of CURRENT to generalize from synthetic training data to in vivo acquisitions was investigated. Results: CURRENT achieved superior spatial SR performance and comparable temporal SR performance to dedicated 4DFlowNet models while providing a unified solution for both tasks. Simultaneous spatiotemporal SR using CURRENT yielded more accurate relative pressure estimates than either spatial or temporal SR alone and outperformed sequential 4DFlowNet-based spatial and temporal SR approaches. Furthermore, the proposed model demonstrated promising generalization to in vivo 4D flow MRI data despite being trained exclusively on synthetic datasets. Conclusion: CURRENT provides a unified framework for spatial and temporal SR of 4D flow MRI. The proposed approach has the potential to enhance physics-based analysis and broaden the applicability of accelerated 4D flow MRI.

papers.title: Finite Blocklength Performance Analysis of Uplink RSMA with Practical Imperfections
papers.abstract: Future generations of wireless networks will support massive communication and hyper-reliable low-latency communications, which are fundamental to large-scale Internet of Things (IoT) deployments with stringent performance requirements. To support such diverse and demanding requirements, robust and flexible multiple access schemes are essential. In this work, we develop a comprehensive analytical framework for evaluating uplink rate-splitting multiple access (RSMA) in the finite blocklength regime under realistic non-ideal conditions. Specifically, we derive closed-form expressions for the block error rate (BLER) and goodput, accounting for imperfect channel state information at the receiver (CSIR), imperfect successive interference cancellation (SIC), and hardware impairments. To reflect practical wireless environments, we model the channel using Nakagami-m fading model. Our analysis shows that at lower transmit power levels, imperfect CSIR is the dominant performance-limiting factor, whereas hardware impairments and imperfect SIC become more significant in degrading system performance as the transmit power increases. To further understand the system behavior, we derive asymptotic BLER expressions. We also analyze the impact of rate allocation, demonstrating its critical role in ensuring fairness and reliability. Monte Carlo simulations validate our analytical expressions. Notably, our results show that uplink RSMA significantly outperforms NOMA even when RSMA operates under harsh imperfect CSIR. This superiority establishes RSMA as a robust and efficient candidate for future wireless networks in practical, constrained environments

papers.title: CV-TF-QKD
papers.abstract: We introduce a continuous-variable version of twin-field quantum key distribution, using independent Gaussian-modulated coherent states and an untrusted single-photon relay. Full-record reconciliation and a binary phase-disclosure protocol achieve nearly equal asymptotic key rates against collective attacks. At fixed weak input-referred excess noise per arm, both rates per relay use scale as $\sqrt{\eta}$, where $\eta$ is the end-to-end transmissivity. For phase disclosure, we establish composable security against general coherent attacks using a bounded test of preparation intensities and sign-parity complementarity. For specified apparatus parameters, finite-key calculations incorporating detector inefficiency, dark counts, phase fluctuations, and reference overhead predict rates exceeding the pure-loss and matched thermal-loss repeaterless bounds. These results extend the twin-field advantage to Gaussian-modulated continuous-variable quantum cryptography.

papers.title: ESDCodec: Ultra-Low Bitrate Speech Codec with Enhanced Semantic Disentanglement and Subband Decoding
papers.abstract: Despite recent advances in neural speech codecs, achieving highfidelity speech reconstruction at low bitrates remains a formidable challenge. To address this limitation, we propose ESDCodec, a speech codec that integrates a thoroughly enhanced semantic quantizer and a conditioned decoder network. Specifically, we employ a randomly initialized and frozen codebook, followed by a lightweight projector, to encode semantic details entirely within a linear space while enhancing codebook utilization. To further improve perceptual quality, we design a condition network that explicitly injects prior subband knowledge into the upsampling decoder. Taking the de-quantized feature as input, this network predicts subband signals, thereby providing fine-grained guidance for waveform reconstruction. Extensive experimental results show that ESDCodec achieves superior reconstruction performance at an ultra-low bitrate of 0.85kbps. For LLM-based speech generation tasks, ESDCodec also consistently outperforms existing codec models.

papers.title: Accelerating matrix-free fast diagonalization and preconditioned linear solvers for higher-order finite element discretized elliptic problems on distributed GPUs
papers.abstract: The time to solution of an iterative solver depends on the number of iterations and the cost per iteration. This paper develops algorithms that reduce both for elliptic problems discretized with high-order continuous finite elements on distributed GPUs, implemented in a unified matrix-free code supporting CUDA, HIP and SYCL. A distributed direct fast-diagonalization (FD) Poisson solver provides exact solutions on tensor-product meshes with direction-wise grading and coefficients varying along one coordinate direction. Its tensor data stay distributed, moved between slab layouts by collective transposes or kept in place by a Schur-complement approach. It is also an exact coarse solver. A two-level hybrid Schwarz preconditioner with FD cell solves (HS-FD) is extended to 2:1 hanging-node octrees with exact local cell inverses, while a \(p\)-multigrid preconditioner with Chebyshev--Jacobi smoothing (CJ-\(p\)MG) resolves hanging-node constraints at every level within fused kernels. Both approaches exploit FP32, where cell shapes and coefficients allow, within an FP64 conjugate-gradient iteration, adaptively select replicated or distributed coarse levels, support block solves for multiple right-hand sides and determine all parameters from the operator without case-specific tuning. Comparisons with Jacobi-preconditioned conjugate gradients (Jacobi PCG), MFEM, nekRS and this http URL span uniform, graded and octree meshes, layered coefficients, and four applications across NVIDIA, AMD and Intel GPUs. The direct solver is two to three orders of magnitude faster than Jacobi PCG on uniform meshes. HS-FD converges in 11 iterations for an octree generalized Poisson problem across 8 to 1024 MI250X graphics compute dies. The results guide solver selection by mesh structure and coefficients

papers.title: Characterization of BNLs 20 and 30 micrometer thick LGADs for the Electron Ion Collider
papers.abstract: The 20 and 30 micrometer thick Low-Gain Avalanche Detectors (LGADs) produced at Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL) were evaluated. Detailed electrical measurements indicate well-formed and stable gain layers with consistently low leakage currents. Transient Current Technique (TCT) was used to evaluate the gain. Fast-laser timing studies demonstrate time resolutions at the level of a few tens of picoseconds. To assess operational longevity under realistic conditions for Electron-Ion Collider sub-detector systems, devices were irradiated with 30 MeV and 60 MeV protons to fluences of 10^13 to 10^14 neq/cm^2, enabling a focused study of radiation-induced effects on gain stability and timing performance.

papers.title: Thermodynamics of words
papers.abstract: We introduce the word thermalization hypothesis according to which in a literary work there are effective interactions between words that drive them to thermalization where their word frequency distribution is the same as for the phenomenon of Rayleigh-Jeans (RJ) thermalization and condensation. In this concept, the different words play a role of classical oscillators (particles) and their word frequencies, or related tokens, are analogous to certain filling factors over energy state levels. The thermalization process is characterized by the conservation of total system energy, or total number of words/tokens, and total probability norm, or total number of different words. We apply this approach to analyze 16 literary works, including Bible, complete works of Shakespeare, and data from American National Corpus. We show that for these cases the effective system energy is very low and thus there is the RJ condensation phenomenon with a big fraction of total probability concentrated at the lowest energy states corresponding to a big fraction of rare words appearing only once or twice in the whole text. Such a RJ condensation is observed for light propagation in multimode optical fibers and other physical systems. We relate the thermalization of words to the recently proposed wealth thermalization for households in world countries. The economy concepts of Lorenz and Pareto curves, and also Zipf curves, are applied to the word frequency distributions of the selected 16 cases and it is shown that the thermalization theory gives a strikingly good description of real data.

papers.title: ScaleBrain: A Scale-Consistent Framework for EEG Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Foundation models pre-trained on large unlabeled electroencephalography (EEG) corpora have emerged as a transformative paradigm for Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) applications. Recent EEG foundation models have shown that multi-scale representations derived from fixed-length patches can improve EEG representation learning. Existing frameworks commonly construct temporal scales through feature-level operations. However, these operations leave the correspondence between learned features and scale-specific characteristics of the original EEG signals implicit. Moreover, when the self-supervised objective is not aligned with the multi-scale input representations, information at some temporal scales may receive insufficient supervision during pre-training. In light of this, we propose ScaleBrain, a scale-consistent pre-training framework that explicitly coordinates multi-scale representations of EEG from both the model input and optimization objective sides. Specifically, ScaleBrain introduces multi-scale EEG tokenization to represent the same EEG segment through analysis windows with different temporal spans and shared temporal anchors, and pairs these representations with scale-specific reconstruction to align with the multi-scale input structure and provide supervision across temporal resolutions during self-supervised learning. We further develop an axial spatio-temporal attention mechanism to contextualize the fused multi-scale representation along spatial and temporal dimensions. Extensive evaluations on six public BCI benchmarks against 12 representative baselines show that ScaleBrain achieves the highest mean Balanced Accuracy on five datasets and ranks third on the remaining one, with only 5.0M parameters, demonstrating strong performance and favorable parameter efficiency.

papers.title: An Alignment Microscope for Imaging Rotational Wavepacket Dynamics
papers.abstract: We introduce a new method for encoding polarization-angle-dependent molecular alignment signals directly into the transverse spatial profile of a femtosecond laser beam. The approach employs a pump-probe setup in a common-path geometry. A radial-azimuthal polarization converter placed in the probe beam produces a doughnut-shaped beam whose local polarization varies continuously with azimuthal angle, thereby encoding the full range of linear polarization orientations from 0 to $2\pi$ within a single transverse beam profile. Consequently, the angular dependence of the molecular response can be recorded simultaneously rather than reconstructed through sequential measurements at different polarization angles. By varying only the pump-probe delay, this spatial encoding enables single-shot acquisition of the complete angular response at each delay and real-time visualization of the evolving molecular alignment pattern as the delay stage is scanned. This technique has enabled the experimental realization of an alignment microscope.

papers.title: How much can a human being lift? A Bayesian latent capability model for Olympic weightlifting
papers.abstract: Estimates of the limits of human performance are usually built on record books, on the premise that a record is the best an athlete could do. In Olympic weightlifting the premise fails, because the competitor declares the weight before each of three attempts per lift and only the heaviest successful attempt is recorded, so a record is a lower bound, chosen by the athlete, on a maximal capability never observed. We treat the maximal lift of each competitor on each competition day as a latent variable, of which every attempt is a trial and every declared weight a measurement. Its distribution at a given bodyweight follows an extreme value mixture model with an estimated threshold, and an athlete-specific random effect links the competitions of each athlete. The model is fitted to the 117,892 attempts of 5,040 athletes in 141 international competitions between 2017 and 2026. The upper tail of capability is bounded, with posterior probability above 0.999 for men, 0.96 for the women's snatch and 0.94 for the women's clean and jerk. At 110 kilograms of bodyweight the men's ceiling lies one to three per cent above the heaviest lifts, against twelve and sixteen per cent for women at 86 kilograms. The record book alone places the men's ceiling six and twelve kilograms higher, because the best lift of a day ending on a success overstates capability.

papers.title: PINNverse meets Jordan--Wigner: learning the Hamiltonian of long spin chains
papers.abstract: Inverse physics-informed neural networks (PINNverse) learn the parameters of a quantum Hamiltonian from measured expectation values, but the network output grows as $4^N$ with the number of qubits $N$. We show that, for spin chains with nearest-neighbor exchange interactions, the Jordan-Wigner transformation removes this exponential cost: the dynamics closes on an $N\times N$ one-body density matrix, so the network needs only $N^2$ outputs and the data are local observables measured in five global settings. Parasitic $ZZ$ couplings (crosstalk) are included through a time-dependent Hartree--Fock closure. With synthetic data, the same network first solves the equation of motion and then recovers the Hamiltonian parameters of chains of up to $50$ qubits, with couplings learned to better than $0.1\%$. Errors in the local frequencies of long chains are removed by a direct least-squares fit started from the network estimate.

papers.title: Safe and Scalable Minimax Adaptive Control of Positive Systems
papers.abstract: This paper studies minimax adaptive control of positive linear systems with fixed unknown dynamics and nonnegative disturbances. We reformulate the problem by compressing the historical data into a vector and a positivity-induced consistency set containing the models compatible with the observations. Together with the physical state, these quantities form a sufficient information state and yield an exact reformulation as a standard minimax dynamic game. We allow the admissible input set to adapt to the current consistency set, ensuring positivity for every remaining feasible model. As inconsistent models are eliminated, the input set can expand, allowing less cautious control actions. For finite model sets, we derive an explicit solution to the Bellman inequality and construct a safe and stabilizing certainty-equivalence controller with robustness guarantees. The framework also accommodates structured classes of continuum model uncertainty whose consistency sets admit fixed, finite-dimensional representations, enabling scalable information-state updates.

papers.title: Passive ladder-network representation of the radiation impedance of a spherical cap on a rigid sphere
papers.abstract: A loudspeaker in a closed box is modeled as a rigid sphere with an axially moving cap. For an axisymmetric cone-velocity profile, its radiation impedance is written as a network. Each spherical-harmonic mode has an impedance rational in frequency, realized exactly as a finite passive ladder of masses and compliances terminated in a resistance. Ideal transformers set by Legendre coefficients couple these ladders; truncated modes reduce to a residual mass. Despite the different geometry, the impedance resembles that of a baffled piston but, at equal volume velocity, has half its low-frequency resistance and about three quarters of its radiation mass.

papers.title: Testing isotropy of random fields with values in abstract spaces
papers.abstract: We study the problem of testing isotropy, i.e., distributional invariance under orthogonal transformations, for random fields taking values in abstract spaces. We propose a novel approach based on computing local directional characteristics, which are uniformly distributed under the assumption of isotropy. Our work is motivated by an application in material science, where we are testing the isotropy of function-valued porosity profiles of paper sheets, whose morphology is resolved by $\mu$-CT imaging. While considerably more general, the presented methodology is competitive with existing isotropy tests for real-valued random fields.

papers.title: A linear programming approach to finite copula interpolation
papers.abstract: We consider exact and interval-valued interpolation of multivariate copulas at arbitrary finite configurations in the unit cube. We first characterize when the prescribed data are compatible with a quasi-copula and derive explicit extremal quasi-copula envelopes. The copula interpolation problem is thereby reduced to a copula sandwich problem between these envelopes. Restricting them to the canonical rectangular grid generated by the data coordinates yields a finite linear feasibility system whose elementary-volume constraints are encoded by a cell--vertex incidence matrix. Farkas' lemma then identifies the criterion of Omladič and Stopar with an explicit certificate of infeasibility. Although this criterion is indexed by infinitely many formal cell combinations, we show that it suffices to test finitely many vertices of a sign-polytopal subdivision. We also extend the construction to $k$-increasing discrete quasi-copulas for $2\leq k\leq d$.

papers.title: Application of the Phase Correction Method in Tracking Modules of Navigation Receivers
papers.abstract: One of the problems of the tracking modules is their significant inertia in case of narrow bandwidth, which is desirable to mitigate signal noise. The paper describes a method of phase correction, improving accuracy and dynamic characteristics of the tracking process in GNSS receivers. The pivotal idea of the method supposes correction of the phase deviation between the received signal and its local copy at the end of every integration period. This correction is performed directly over the phase accumulator of a DDS system. This approach reduces inertial effects crucially. Application of phase correction method with narrow filter bandwidth is much more efficient when FLL-assisted PLL tracking is used. It is shown that in this case a separate FLL discriminator is not needed, and the resulting filter structure can be significantly simplified.

papers.title: Spatio-Temporal Calibration of a Vehicle-Mounted Microphone Array for Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: Microphones let an autonomous vehicle sense into areas its cameras and LiDAR cannot see, by picking up the sound that other traffic participants emit. Locating those sources and fusing them with the visual perception requires the microphone array to be calibrated and registered relative to the vehicle's other sensors. Existing calibration methods assume small, unobstructed indoor rigs, whereas a vehicle body casts an acoustic shadow that straight-line propagation cannot represent, and to our knowledge no calibration of an array distributed around a vehicle has been reported. We propose a pipeline that uses a balloon burst as a single cross-modal target, which the LiDAR locates in metric coordinates, every microphone hears as a sharp onset and a camera times. Each observation is weighted by its own timing variance, which discounts shadowed arrivals instead of discarding them and needs no model of the vehicle. On a full-size vehicle with eight microphones over a 4.9 m aperture, the held-out range residual of 6.37 cm approaches the 6.07 cm floor set by the onset timing noise, and the calibrated array tracks a moving source to within a few degrees of the vehicle's own LiDAR. A dozen bursts spread around the vehicle suffice, and spreading them matters more than adding more.

papers.title: DynamAuction: A Reinforcement Learning Environment for Repeated Auctions with Dynamic Value
papers.abstract: A buyer who repeatedly participates in auctions for related items often faces a dynamic value problem: what they win today changes what tomorrow's items are worth. Despite the empirical importance of such effects, especially in display advertising, the algorithmic literature on repeated auctions has largely focused on the learning problem, by treating each opportunity as a contextual bandit, while sidestepping the planning problem induced by the dependence of current value on past wins. We introduce DynamAuction, a synthetic environment for single-buyer sequential bidding. The reward from each win depends on the buyer's history of previous wins, summarized through a carry-over state. The environment supports first- and second-price auctions, non-homogeneous Poisson arrivals, delayed feedback, saturation, and recency effects. We also introduce a new class of Model Predictive Control (MPC) algorithms. On our benchmark scenario, these MPC policies outperform off-the-shelf deep RL baselines (PPO, SAC, TD3) as well as a tuned shading baseline. We release DynamAuction to support RL research on repeated auctions.

papers.title: The Feynman Dyson argument extended to the inhomogeneous Maxwell equations
papers.abstract: The Feynman-Dyson argument gives the homogeneous Maxwell equations but does not identify the sources in the other two equations with the charge and current carried by matter. Taking the homogeneous equations as given, we derive Gauss's law and the Ampere-Maxwell law for the sources entering the Lorentz force and the power delivered to matter. We assume, in particular, that the field densities and fluxes are at most quadratic in the fields and covariant under proper rotations. We require the same expressions for the sources to satisfy local energy and momentum conservation for every field that obeys the homogeneous equations, and to be continuous in spacetime along every smooth such field. The charge and current densities are then unique up to the values of $\varepsilon_0$ and $\mu_0$. We also discuss how these assumptions might be relaxed.

papers.title: On the information rate of phones, syllables and words
papers.abstract: Which linguistic units minimise the bitrate required to encode speech content: phones, syllables, words, maybe larger units, or something in between? This question has implications for the development of speech and language systems and theories of human language processing. Using a transcribed corpus of 960 hours of English audiobooks, I compare the information rates of phones, syllables, words, multi-word combinations and intermediate tokenisations. While all units are equivalent under a perfect language model, it makes sense to compare these under limited modelling budgets; I use $n$-gram and transformer language models. The lowest bitrates are achieved using words, with slightly longer units sometimes performing best. The results show that, when modelling capacity is limited, units larger than syllables but smaller than long multi-word phrases provide the most efficient representation in terms of information rate.

papers.title: Beyond Fourier and Laplace: The Hankel Neural Operator for Learning Solution Operators of Differential Equations
papers.abstract: Fourier and Laplace neural operators (FNO, LNO) learn kernel integral operators in a transform domain evaluated on a periodic grid. FNO has no explicit mechanism for boundaries, initial states or transients; LNO adds pole--residue symbols but evaluates them on the discrete Fourier grid with unconstrained poles. FNO's error is large on undamped oscillators and grows under grid refinement. We introduce the Hankel neural operator (HNO), derived from the structure of the solution operator. We prove that the solution operator of a well-posed linear constant-coefficient boundary-value problem on an interval is a Toeplitz operator with a rational kernel plus a finite-rank Hankel-type operator carrying boundary information. Classical results of Kronecker, Nehari and Adamyan--Arov--Krein characterise this kernel class: stable poles, finite Hankel rank and norm bounds independent of the interval length. HNO realises the class in three ways: a non-periodic convolution evaluated by the FFT, with a causal form; a closed-loop Lur'e operator for dynamics without fading memory; and a rational Fourier multiplier that contains FNO as a special case. Trained from data alone, HNO has the lowest mean test error on all nine LNO benchmarks and on the Burgers, Darcy and Navier--Stokes benchmarks of FNO; two of these differences, and the Navier--Stokes comparison with a parameter-matched FNO, are not statistically significant. On the six ODE problems it lowers the better baseline's mean error 2.1--5.2 times, and its Darcy error stays nearly constant from $85^2$ to $421^2$ grids, where FNO's grows eightfold. Ablations support each component. Code and data: \hnorepo{}.

papers.title: Distributionally Robust Indirect-Feedback Stochastic MPC with Gelbrich Ambiguity Sets
papers.abstract: Stochastic model predictive control uses disturbance statistics to set safety margins. Errors in these statistics can invalidate the safety guarantees. This paper therefore describes the uncertainty in the disturbance mean and covariance by a prescribed Gelbrich ambiguity set. This contains distributions of any shape whose moments are close in the Gelbrich distance to the nominal values, including distributions with unbounded support. For linear time-invariant systems with additive disturbances, we build on the indirect feedback paradigm, propagate this moment uncertainty along the error dynamics, and obtain a closed-form constraint tightening that is computed offline. Robustness enters as a single additive term that grows with the size of the ambiguity set, so the online problem remains a quadratic program. Recursive feasibility and closed-loop satisfaction of conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) constraints hold for every disturbance distribution in the set. We illustrate the method on a linearized planar quadrotor.

papers.title: Excitable Behaviours of a First-Order High-Pass Neuron Model
papers.abstract: With the rise of neuromorphic technologies, simple and tunable neuron models are needed to analyse and design spiking systems. However, the simplest neuron models, e.g., Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) models, usually fail to capture the excitable behaviours of biological neurons. This could be a significant limitation, as excitability enables reliable spike timing under parametric uncertainties. Recently, a minimal excitable model, the so-called High-Pass Model (HPM), was introduced in neuroengineering. It simply consists of a static sigmoid with a high-pass filter in positive feedback. Given its novelty, it is still unclear how easily the HPM can be tuned, and how much of the excitable behaviours of a biophysical neuron it can reproduce. To address these questions, we investigate the tunability of a first-order HPM sub- and supra-rheobase, i.e., below and above the onset of the tonic spiking regime (where the neuron spikes periodically), and compare its behaviours with those of a simple Hodgkin-Huxley-type Conductance-Based Model (CBM). Below rheobase, both models fire spikes in response to transient inputs, including post-inhibitory rebound spikes. Above rheobase, an affine reparametrization of the input of the HPM suffices to fit its frequency-current curve to that of a CBM. The two models mostly differ near their respective rheobases, where the first-order HPM lacks bistability and spike latency. We suggest that modifying the frequency-selective element of the HPM may be sufficient to overcome this limitation. These results highlight the potential of the HPM as a fundamental computational primitive in neuromorphic, spike-based technologies.

papers.title: Analytic Two-Radius Model for the Zero-Shear and High-Frequency Viscosity of Colloidal Suspensions
papers.abstract: Nearly hard-sphere colloids are stabilized by short-range repulsions that set their effective size and equilibrium microstructure. Their hydrodynamic interactions, in contrast, are set by the no-slip surface. Since these two do not necessarily coincide, there are potentially two effective radii that control their dynamics in different ways. Yet it is commonplace to model and analyze such suspensions with a single effective radius, which merges these different physics. Two-radius models, in which a hard, solvent-permeable shell surrounds a no-slip core, have been proposed to improve the description of these suspensions. Their rheology is known exactly at pair level, but at higher concentrations their zero-shear viscosity has been obtained only with semi-empirical expressions, which do not recover the exact pair result. Here, we close this gap with a theory for the zero-shear and high-frequency viscosity of these two-radius models. By keeping pairs out of near contact, the shell lowers the high-frequency viscosity, as our Stokesian dynamics simulations confirm, and shifts the zero-shear viscosity from hydrodynamic toward thermodynamic stress. We apply our theory to experiments on charge- and sterically stabilized colloids from the literature and find that it accurately describes the measured viscosities. We discuss the benefits of fitting data to a two-radius model compared to a single-radius one. To facilitate this fitting in future work, closed-form expressions are provided that cover the full range of shell thicknesses and volume fractions.

papers.title: Frequency Comb as a Probe of Fluctuation Mechanisms in Nanomechanical Systems
papers.abstract: Frequency combs are indispensable in metrology. We show that a frequency comb also probes frequency fluctuations of the system. In our nanomechanical resonator, the comb arises from self-sustained vibrations of a resonantly driven nonlinear mode. The comb lineshapes reveal exponentially correlated (Ornstein--Uhlenbeck) frequency noise. Its correlation time agrees with the independently measured relaxation time of the vibrations. The noise leads to anomalous phase diffusion. Its mechanism is generic: like the comb itself, it stems from the strong nonlinearity of the self-sustained vibrations.

papers.title: On the Spectral Estimation of VARMA Processes
papers.abstract: We consider the problem of estimating the power spectral density of a Vector-valued Autoregressive Moving-Average (VARMA) process. A well-established approach to accomplishing this task consists of formulating a moment problem that selects the spectral density maximizing an entropy-like index while matching certain moments of the underlying process. However, existing methods assume that the moving-average (MA) component is either fixed or scalar, thereby reducing the class of ARMA models over which the optimal spectral density is sought. In this paper, we propose a new moment problem, based on the notion of transportation entropy, for learning the spectral density of a VARMA process without fixing the MA component or restricting it to be scalar.

papers.title: TransGHOST: Real-Time, Synthesis-Free Reconstruction of Instrument-Occluded Regions in Ophthalmic Microsurgery
papers.abstract: Intraoperative scene perception in ophthalmic microsurgery is limited by instrument occlusion: when a tool enters the high-magnification field, it conceals tissue from both the surgeon and the perception components of robot-assisted systems that process the video. Generative inpainting can remove the occluder but replaces the missing image content with synthesis, which is unsuitable when visual provenance matters. Many video inpainters also depend on future frames and cannot operate online. We present TransGHOST, a causal reference-guided reconstruction pipeline whose non-generative safe mode operates in real time. Every restored value is obtained by resampling a recorded frame using geometric transforms fitted only to visible regions. The system provides per-pixel confidence and provenance and marks unsupported pixels as abstentions. We evaluate TransGHOST on a new veterinary clinical corpus of canine cataract surgery with pixel-level instrument and anatomy labels. Only the occluded region is scored, and each scoring target is verified to differ from the reference supplied to the system. Safe mode reaches 31.89 dB masked PSNR and 0.915 masked SSIM at 51.7 ms median and 85.5 ms 95th-percentile latency. On a pre-declared held-out cohort using instrument cutouts excluded from segmentation training, it reaches 29.83 dB masked PSNR, while matched-mask evaluation on validation shows a 3.45 dB advantage over LaMa. Region-aware reference selection improves masked PSNR by 3.60 dB over recency when candidate references can themselves be occluded. Reference-age analysis further defines the operating interval for the brief, repeated occlusions targeted by TransGHOST.

papers.title: Counterfactual Analysis of Extent Leakage from Annotation-Derived Prompts in Vision-Language Medical Image Segmentation
papers.abstract: Text-guided segmentation models receive an image and a short caption about the lesion, and on public benchmarks the caption improves accuracy considerably. On colonoscopy and breast ultrasound, however, the size, count and location words of each caption were computed from the mask that later scores the prediction, and the chest X-ray captions were written by benchmark annotators. We tested what two published models take from them. On colonoscopy and chest X-ray, it is mostly the lesion's extent. Keeping only the size word or the lung-zone phrase recovers 84 to 98 percent of the improvement over an empty caption, and removing it loses 52 to 77 percent. The rest matters little, and a polyp called a rock is segmented just as well. We call this extent leakage. On breast ultrasound, nearly half the captions also name the diagnosis, which carries part of the benefit. Retraining on three datasets shows that models pick up this habit from their training captions, though only partly on breast ultrasound, and that it weakens their segmentation from the image alone. The leak can be measured without training a model, since caption words alone predict lesion area (coefficient of determination 0.54 to 0.77 on six of seven test sets). Without the test mask, the best method we tested, which estimates extent from the image, reaches 74.59 Dice on colonoscopy against the published 77.23. We propose an evaluation protocol that keeps what a caption says about the image apart from what it copies from the label.

papers.title: Rheology of Parametric Odd Materials
papers.abstract: The design and control of rheological properties in active systems are crucial for developing functional materials with novel properties. While significant attention has been devoted to odd viscosity and odd elasticity, comprehensive odd rheological models remain scarce. Here, we introduce and characterise a platform-agnostic odd viscoelastic material, where complex responses arise from parametric control of internal rotational degrees of freedom and are triggered by coupling between normal and shear stresses. Such control can be achieved through either parametric driving or a parametric nonlinear feedback. We further show that this coupling can induce rotation-driven fluidisation, transitioning the material from an elasticity-dominated to a viscosity-dominated regime. Lastly, we show that the interplay between odd and even sectors enhances the nonlinear material response under large-amplitude oscillatory shear (LAOS). The findings outline a route to Floquet-engineered metafluids with programmable, non-reciprocal rheology.

papers.title: Design of Self-Folding Origami Architectures for Biomedical Implants: A Finite Element Simulation Framework
papers.abstract: Minimally invasive brain implants require compact deployment geometries and controlled shape transformation for delivery through confined vessels. Origami-inspired structures enable large shape changes from compact to tailored deployed configurations, but implementation at microscale dimensions remains challenging, as conventional designs rely on predefined mountain and valley folds that become increasingly difficult to fabricate and assemble as unit-cell size is reduced to meet clinical requirements. To address this, we propose a self-folding methodology based on thermally induced stresses in thin-film bimetallic composites. Pairing the shape memory alloy Nitinol (NiTi) with molybdenum or stainless steel (SS316L) exploits their differing thermal expansion coefficients to generate localized hinge bending, enabling deterministic, autonomous folding into prescribed mountain and valley configurations. Using finite element simulations, we systematically optimize hinge length, layer thickness, width, and shape, identifying a hinge geometry achieving a ~50% reduction in unit-cell dimensions relative to previously reported designs. Integration into a complete waterbomb origami unit cell confirms that the strip-level folding mechanism scales to produce coordinated, self-folding deformation across the tessellated structure. These results demonstrate the feasibility of stress-induced, self-folding thin-film origami architectures built from clinically established biomaterials, providing a scalable design framework for next-generation, active neurovascular implants with integrated sensing and monitoring functionality.

papers.title: Deceleration without identification: testing a power-law trend in Bitcoin prices under persistent noise
papers.abstract: Plotted against time since its first block on logarithmic axes, the price of Bitcoin lies close to a straight line, and a power law in time has been proposed as its long-run trend. A good fit is weak evidence: when deviations from a trend are as persistent as a random walk, regressions on time find trends and high $R^2$ where none exist. We first bound what fifteen years of weekly prices can reveal, then test only what is answerable. Using a few low-frequency averages, invariant to the noise scale and calibrated over a declared family of persistent deviations with a four-year cycle and declining volatility, we test constant drift in expected log price against an added log-age term. The procedure was fixed, validated and publicly hashed before it was applied once. Constant drift is rejected under this family at nominal 5%, and a log-age coefficient of 5.7, close to the published exponent, is not rejected. The rejection does not survive allowing persistence beyond a random walk, and a Gompertz curve with a ceiling fits about as well as the power law. Whether deviations revert to the trend cannot be decided. Registered forecasts for 2027-2030 will be scored by future prices.

papers.title: Data-driven regional traffic simulation from heterogeneous mobility sources
papers.abstract: Regional traffic simulators increasingly combine mobile-phone, road-sensor and GPS data, but what each source contributes is rarely clear. We present an agent-based simulator of daily traffic in Emilia-Romagna, Italy: phone data give trips and their timing, half of the road sensors set the traffic level, all sensors correct it locally, and GPS traces guide route choice. We measure what each source adds against predictors without simulation, on sensors kept out of parameter calibration in winter 2020 and partly shared with it in summer 2021; as these sensors informed some modelling choices, the evaluation is not fully independent. Total traffic is within 1% of observations in winter and 10% in summer, and the simulator ranks roads better than a road-type predictor (Spearman 0.67-0.68 against 0.41-0.48, winter). GPS improves this ranking, sensors improve local estimates, and timing comes mostly from the demand. Single-road errors remain similar to those of simple predictors, and the test of specific origin-destination pairings was underpowered and inconclusive. These findings provide a practical framework for assessing the contribution and limitations of heterogeneous data sources in regional traffic simulation.

papers.title: Chiral magnon Kerr interaction from linear and nonlinear Meissner screening in ferromagnet--superconductor bilayers
papers.abstract: Magnon Kerr interaction showing a dependence of magnon dispersion frequency on its population is a useful functionality for nonlinear and quantum magnonics; its strength and sign depend on magnetic anisotropy, bias, and mode geometry. We here propose to use a superconducting gate to tune the Kerr interaction of magnons in ferromagnetic insulators. Even when the superconductor responds linearly, the frequency shift induced by its reflected dipolar field depends on the longitudinal magnetization. The decrease of this magnetization with increasing precession amplitude therefore produces a Kerr contribution.
